title: The Lotus
hook: the Lotus of the True Law: a sutra of parables, visions and one great promise
carry: the lotus of the true law

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Diamond Sutra ended on its closing verse: look on the world like stars, like dew, like a bubble, like lightning. Your line: like dew, like lightning. Did you catch one thing passing? Day one thousand one hundred fifty.

A lotus puts its roots down in pond mud. Dark, soft, a little smelly. The stem climbs up through murky water. And then, above the surface, the flower opens clean, as if it had never touched any of it. The Diamond Sutra was a blade: short, sharp, cutting away every grip. The next text on this path works in a completely different key. It tells stories. It stages visions the size of the sky. And it carries one promise so large that the people in the story don't believe it at first. It takes its name from that flower. Today: the Lotus.
screen: `ROOTS IN THE MUD.` → `A FLOWER ABOVE THE WATER.` → `FROM A BLADE TO A STORY.`

segments.voice: First, the name. In Sanskrit the sutra is called the Saddharmapundarika. The scholar H. Kern, translating it from Sanskrit into English, rendered the title as the Lotus of the True Law. Saddharma, the true Dharma, the true teaching. Pundarika, the lotus. So the title holds both the teaching and the flower. Second, why a lotus. The image isn't new to this sutra. In a discourse in the Pali canon, the Buddha compares himself to a lotus: born in the water, grown up in the water, it rises above the water and stands there unsoiled by it. In the same way, he says, he was born in the world and grew up in the world, yet lives unsoiled by it. Mud below, flower above, one plant. Third, what's inside. The Lotus is a sutra of parables. A father calling his children out of a burning house. A son who ran away and comes home not knowing he's the heir. A rain that falls on every kind of plant. A jewel sewn into a sleeping friend's robe. And it's a sutra of visions: a ray of light from the Buddha's brow, a jeweled stupa rising out of the earth, bodhisattvas springing up from the ground. Fourth, the promise. Running through all of it is one great claim: that the Buddha's teachings, however many shapes they take, lead toward one goal, and that those listening will themselves become Buddhas. The sutra shows people hearing this and being stunned. Some East Asian schools, among them Tiantai in China and Tendai and Nichiren in Japan, place it at the center of their practice, and in Nichiren Buddhism the title itself is chanted. Over the coming weeks, this path walks through it story by story.
screen: `THE TEACHING AND THE FLOWER.` · `UNSOILED BY THE WATER.` · `PARABLES AND VISIONS.` · `ONE GREAT PROMISE.` · then, large: `THE LOTUS OF THE TRUE LAW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: read one parable's title. Settle, and breathe. Let a few of the Lotus's pictures pass slowly through your mind, one per breath. The burning house. The son who came home. The rain on all the plants. The jewel in the robe. Don't reach for the stories yet; most of them come later on this path. Just notice which picture draws you. Then stay with that one: let it sit in front of you like a closed book with a good cover, waiting to be opened. The bell holds the time.
Saddharmapundarika. The Lotus Sutra's Sanskrit name: the lotus of the true Dharma, which Kern rendered the Lotus of the True Law. Today's word.
Your line: the lotus of the true law. Today, notice one good thing that's growing out of a muddy situation in your life, and give it a second look. Day one thousand one hundred fifty.

howItsDone: The Lotus Sutra is chanted, copied and studied in Mahayana communities in East Asia and beyond; Tiantai and Tendai Buddhists center their teaching on it, and in Nichiren Buddhism practitioners chant its title.

fork.setup: a lotus is born in the water and grows up in the water. in the Buddha's simile, what does it do next?
options: rises above the water and stands unsoiled by it
pulls up its roots and floats away
fork.reveal: it rises above the water, unsoiled; so the Buddha says he grew up in the world and lives unsoiled by it.

original.note: Sanskrit: the Lotus Sutra's title; saddharma, the true Dharma, and pundarika, the lotus.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Lotus Sutra is a book about flowers.
what it means: the lotus names the true teaching, rising clean out of the world; inside are parables, visions and a promise.
what a scholar hears: Kern's English, made from the Sanskrit, titles it the Lotus of the True Law; East Asian schools such as Tiantai, Tendai and Nichiren center on it.

Lotus simile paraphrased from SN 22.94 (also AN 4.36 has a lotus simile); confirm the reference.

Parables and visions listed (burning house, lost son, rain on plants, jewel in the robe, ray from the brow, jeweled stupa rising from the earth, bodhisattvas springing from the ground) should all appear in Kern; confirm.

'Schools such as Tiantai in China and Tendai and Nichiren in Japan have built their practice around it' and 'in the Nichiren schools the title itself is chanted' are claims not stated in the cited text (the outline's block note says something similar); confirm or soften.
